q: The earth ______ round the sun.
exp: Universal truths and scientific facts are always expressed in the Simple Present Tense ('moves').

q: She ______ to Patna yesterday.
exp: Past time markers like 'yesterday', 'ago', and 'last night' take the Simple Past Tense ('went').

q: It ______ raining since morning.
exp: An action that started in the past and is still continuing ('since morning') uses the Present Perfect Continuous Tense ('has been').

q: The patient ______ before the doctor arrived.
exp: When two actions occur in the past, the earlier action takes Past Perfect ('had died') and the later takes Simple Past ('arrived').

q: Look! The birds ______ in the sky.
exp: Words like 'Look!' and 'Listen!' indicate an action happening right now, requiring Present Continuous ('are flying').

q: If it ______, we shall stay at home.
exp: In Type-1 conditional sentences, the 'if' clause takes Simple Present ('rains') while the main clause takes Simple Future.

q: I ______ this book for two hours.
exp: 'For two hours' with a continuing action calls for Present Perfect Continuous ('have been reading').

q: He ______ his homework just now.
exp: Adverbs like 'just', 'just now', 'already', and 'yet' are typically used with the Present Perfect Tense ('has finished').

q: When I reached the station, the train ______.
exp: The train's departure happened prior to reaching the station, so Past Perfect ('had already left') is used.

q: My father ______ newspaper every morning.
exp: Habitual or daily actions ('every morning') are expressed in the Simple Present Tense ('reads').

q: They ______ cricket in the field at this moment.
exp: 'At this moment' shows an ongoing present activity, taking Present Continuous ('are playing').

q: By next year, she ______ her graduation.
exp: 'By + future time' ('By next year') indicates completion before a future point, using Future Perfect ('will have completed').

q: I wish I ______ a king!
exp: Unreal wishes after 'I wish' always take the subjunctive 'were' regardless of the subject.

q: While she was cooking, the phone ______.
exp: A sudden past action interrupting an ongoing past activity takes the Simple Past Tense ('rang').

q: We ______ in this village since 2010.
exp: 'Since 2010' indicates duration from a specific point in the past up to now, requiring 'have been living'.

q: Columbus ______ America in 1492.
exp: Completed historical events with a specific past date take the Simple Past Tense ('discovered').

q: She ______ a letter when I entered her room.
exp: An action in progress at a specific moment in the past takes Past Continuous ('was writing').

q: He ______ to Delhi tomorrow.
exp: 'Tomorrow' indicates a future action, requiring Simple Future Tense ('will go').

q: Water ______ at 100 degrees Celsius.
exp: Scientific laws and general truths use Simple Present Tense ('boils').

q: Have you ever ______ the Taj Mahal?
exp: After 'have/has/had', the past participle (V3) form 'seen' is always used.

q: He usually ______ tea in the morning.
exp: Frequency adverbs like 'usually', 'always', and 'often' indicate Simple Present Tense ('takes').

q: The baby ______ because it is hungry now.
exp: The word 'now' denotes an action happening right at the moment of speaking, using 'is crying'.

q: If I had worked hard, I ______ the examination.
exp: In Type-3 conditional sentences ('If + had + V3'), the main clause takes 'would have + V3'.

q: She ______ her keys; she cannot open the door.
exp: A past action whose result is visible in the present uses Present Perfect ('has lost').

q: Honesty ______ the best policy.
exp: Proverbs and timeless truths are always expressed in the Simple Present Tense ('is').

q: Two and two ______ four.
exp: Mathematical facts take Simple Present Tense ('makes').

q: I ______ him for ten years.
exp: Stative verbs like 'know' are not used in continuous tenses; with 'for ten years', Present Perfect ('have known') is used.

q: The train ______ at 6:00 AM daily.
exp: Fixed timetables and daily schedules use Simple Present Tense ('leaves').

q: Last night I ______ a strange dream.
exp: 'Last night' denotes a finished past event, taking Simple Past ('saw').

q: They ______ the bridge before the monsoon begins.
exp: Completion of an action before another future event uses Future Perfect ('will have built').

q: He talks as if he ______ everything.
exp: After 'as if' or 'as though' expressing unreal situations, the Simple Past ('knew') is used.

q: We ______ our lunch an hour ago.
exp: The word 'ago' is always used with the Simple Past Tense ('finished').

q: It is time we ______ home.
exp: The structure 'It is time / It is high time + subject' is always followed by the Simple Past Tense ('went').

q: Listen! Someone ______ at the door.
exp: 'Listen!' draws attention to an immediate ongoing action, requiring Present Continuous ('is knocking').

q: She ______ ill since last Sunday.
exp: 'Since last Sunday' requires Present Perfect ('has been') for stative adjectives like 'ill'.

q: I ______ a letter to my friend right now.
exp: 'Right now' indicates the Present Continuous Tense ('am writing').

q: India ______ independence in 1947.
exp: A specific year in the past ('1947') takes the Simple Past Tense ('got').

q: When I was a child, I ______ football every evening.
exp: Past habits are expressed using the Simple Past Tense ('played').

q: Neither of the boys ______ present yesterday.
exp: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb, and 'yesterday' requires the past form 'was'.

q: By the time you arrive, I ______ sleeping.
exp: An action that will be in progress at a future moment uses Future Continuous ('will be sleeping').

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Ram writes a letter.'
options: A letter was written by Ram.
A letter is written by Ram.
A letter is being written by Ram.
A letter has been written by Ram.
exp: Simple Present Active (V1/V5) changes into 'is/am/are + V3' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She is singing a sweet song.'
options: A sweet song is sung by her.
A sweet song is being sung by her.
A sweet song was being sung by her.
A sweet song has been sung by her.
exp: Present Continuous Active ('is/am/are + V-ing') changes to 'is/am/are + being + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'He has completed the work.'
options: The work is completed by him.
The work has been completed by him.
The work had been completed by him.
The work was completed by him.
exp: Present Perfect Active ('has/have + V3') takes 'been' before V3 in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The police arrested the thief.'
options: The thief is arrested by the police.
The thief was arrested by the police.
The thief had been arrested by the police.
The thief was being arrested by the police.
exp: Simple Past Active (V2) changes into 'was/were + V3' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'They were playing football.'
options: Football was being played by them.
Football were being played by them.
Football is being played by them.
exp: Past Continuous Active ('was/were + V-ing') changes into 'was/were + being + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She had already cooked the food.'
options: The food was already cooked by her.
The food had already been cooked by her.
The food has already been cooked by her.
The food is already cooked by her.
exp: Past Perfect Active ('had + V3') becomes 'had been + V3' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'I shall help you.'
options: You will be helped by me.
You would be helped by me.
You have been helped by me.
exp: Simple Future Active ('shall/will + V1') changes into 'will/shall + be + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Open the door.'
exp: Imperative sentences expressing a command are changed into passive using 'Let + object + be + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Help the poor.'
exp: Imperative sentences giving moral advice use 'Object + should be + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Please give me a pen.'
options: Let a pen be given to me.
You are requested to give me a pen.
You are ordered to give me a pen.
A pen is given to me.
exp: Sentences starting with 'Please' or 'Kindly' change into 'You are requested to + V1...'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Who wrote the Ramayana?'
options: By whom was the Ramayana written?
By whom is the Ramayana written?
By who the Ramayana was written?
exp: 'Who' changes to 'By whom' followed by auxiliary verb + subject + V3.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'I know him.'
options: He has been known by me.
exp: The verb 'know' is always followed by the preposition 'to' instead of 'by' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'His behaviour surprised me.'
options: I was surprised by his behaviour.
I was surprised at his behaviour.
I am surprised with his behaviour.
I was surprised to his behaviour.
exp: Verbs like 'surprised', 'astonished', and 'amazed' take 'at' instead of 'by' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Smoke filled the room.'
options: The room was filled by smoke.
The room was filled with smoke.
The room is filled with smoke.
The room had filled with smoke.
exp: 'Filled' takes the preposition 'with' rather than 'by' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'People speak English all over the world.'
options: English was spoken all over the world.
English is spoken all over the world.
English is being spoken all over the world.
English has been spoken all over the world.
exp: Vague agents like 'people', 'someone', and 'they' are omitted in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Someone has stolen my watch.'
exp: 'Someone' is omitted, and Present Perfect Active becomes 'has been stolen'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Can you lift this heavy box?'
options: Can this heavy box lifted by you?
Can this heavy box be lifted by you?
Could this heavy box be lifted by you?
Is this heavy box lifted by you?
exp: Modal verbs ('can, may, must, should') take 'be + V3' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'We must respect our elders.'
options: Our elders must respected by us.
Our elders should be respected by us.
Our elders are respected by us.
exp: Modal 'must + V1' changes to 'must be + V3' in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She gave me a book.'
options: I was given a book by her.
A book is given to me by her.
I am given a book by her.
A book was being given to me by her.
exp: In double-object sentences, either the indirect object ('I') or direct object ('a book') can become the passive subject.

q: Choose the correct active voice: 'A letter is being written by Sita.'
exp: 'Is being written' converts back to Present Continuous Active ('is writing').

q: Choose the correct active voice: 'The tiger was killed by the hunter.'
options: The hunter had killed the tiger.
The hunter is killing the tiger.
exp: 'Was killed' converts back to Simple Past Active ('killed').

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Honey tastes sweet.'
options: Honey is sweet when it is tasted.
exp: Quasi-passive verbs like 'taste', 'smell', and 'feel' follow the structure 'Subject + be + adjective + when + pronoun + be + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Rose smells sweet.'
options: Rose is sweet when it is smelt.
exp: Quasi-passive construction changes 'Rose smells sweet' into 'Rose is sweet when it is smelt'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Do not insult the weak.'
options: Let the weak not be insulted.
Do not let the weak insulted.
exp: Negative imperative sentences change to 'Let + object + not + be + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Why did you beat him?'
options: Why was he beaten by you?
Why is he beaten by you?
Why he was beaten by you?
Why were he beaten by you?
exp: Interrogative Simple Past ('did + V1') becomes 'was/were + subject + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The teacher is teaching the students.'
options: The students are taught by the teacher.
The students are being taught by the teacher.
The students were being taught by the teacher.
The students have been taught by the teacher.
exp: Plural subject 'The students' takes 'are being taught'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'I have to do this work.'
options: This work has to be done by me.
This work have to be done by me.
This work had to be done by me.
This work is to be done by me.
exp: Infinitive 'to + V1' changes into 'to be + V3', and singular 'This work' takes 'has'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She made me laugh.'
options: I was made laugh by her.
I was made to laugh by her.
I am made to laugh by her.
I was making to laugh by her.
exp: Bare infinitives after 'make' take 'to' ('to laugh') when converted into Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'They will have finished the project.'
options: The project will be finished by them.
The project will have been finished by them.
The project would have been finished by them.
The project has been finished by them.
exp: Future Perfect Active ('will have + V3') changes to 'will have been + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Did he buy a new car?'
options: Was a new car bought by him?
Is a new car bought by him?
Were a new car bought by him?
Had a new car bought by him?
exp: Simple Past interrogative 'Did... buy' changes to 'Was + object + bought'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Who teaches you English?'
options: By whom are you taught English?
By whom is you taught English?
By whom were you taught English?
exp: 'Who' becomes 'By whom' and 'you' takes 'are taught'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'One should keep one's promises.'
options: One's promises should be kept by one.
exp: Indefinite pronoun 'one' is omitted in Passive Voice, yielding 'Promises should be kept'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'It is time to close the shop.'
options: It is time for the shop to be closed.
It is time the shop is closed.
It is time to be closed the shop.
exp: The pattern 'It is time to + V1 + object' changes to 'It is time for + object + to be + V3'.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She is going to buy a house.'
options: A house is going to be bought by her.
A house was going to be bought by her.
A house is being bought by her.
A house has been bought by her.
exp: 'Going to + V1' changes into 'going to be + V3'.

q: Choose the correct active voice: 'My pocket has been picked.'
exp: When the agent is unknown, 'Someone' is supplied in Active Voice ('Someone has picked my pocket').

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The news pleased us.'
options: We were pleased by the news.
We were pleased with the news.
We are pleased at the news.
We were pleased to the news.
exp: 'Pleased' takes 'with' in Passive Voice when referring to something or someone.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Are you reading a novel?'
options: Is a novel read by you?
Is a novel being read by you?
Was a novel being read by you?
Are a novel being read by you?
exp: Singular 'a novel' takes 'Is... being read' in Present Continuous Passive.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Nobody can solve this puzzle.'
options: This puzzle can be solved by nobody.
This puzzle could not be solved.
exp: 'Nobody' converts into a negative verb ('cannot be solved') in Passive Voice.

q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Kindly post this letter.'
options: You are requested to post this letter.
You are ordered to post this letter.
exp: 'Kindly' indicates a polite request, changing to 'You are requested to...'.

q: Which of the following tenses CANNOT be changed into Passive Voice?
exp: Perfect Continuous tenses (Present, Past, Future) and Future Continuous do not have standard passive forms.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said, 'I am busy now.'
options: He said that he is busy now.
He said that he was busy then.
He said that I was busy then.
He told that he was busy now.
exp: Reporting verb 'said' is in past tense, so 'am' changes to 'was', 'I' to 'he', and 'now' to 'then'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said to me, 'You are my best friend.'
options: She told me that I was her best friend.
She said me that you were my best friend.
She told me that I am her best friend.
She asked me that I was her best friend.
exp: 'Said to' changes to 'told', 'you' changes according to the object 'me' to 'I', and 'my' changes to 'her'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: The teacher said, 'The earth moves round the sun.'
options: The teacher said that the earth moved round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun.
The teacher told that the earth had moved round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth is moving round the sun.
exp: Universal truths and scientific facts never change their tense in indirect speech.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: Ram said to Sita, 'I will help you tomorrow.'
options: Ram told Sita that he would help her the next day.
Ram told Sita that he will help her tomorrow.
Ram said Sita that he would help you the next day.
Ram told Sita that I would help her the next day.
exp: 'Will' becomes 'would', 'you' becomes 'her', and 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said, 'I bought a new car yesterday.'
options: He said that he bought a new car the previous day.
He said that he had bought a new car the previous day.
He said that he has bought a new car yesterday.
He said that he had bought a new car yesterday.
exp: Simple Past ('bought') shifts to Past Perfect ('had bought') and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said to him, 'Are you going to Patna?'
options: She asked him that was he going to Patna.
She asked him if he was going to Patna.
She told him if he is going to Patna.
She asked him whether was he going to Patna.
exp: Yes/No interrogative sentences use 'asked' and conjunction 'if' or 'whether', followed by assertive word order.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said to me, 'Where do you live?'
options: He asked me where did I live.
He asked me where I lived.
He asked me that where I lived.
He told me where I live.
exp: In Wh-questions, the Wh-word itself acts as a connector and the sentence becomes assertive ('where I lived').

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: The doctor said to the patient, 'Take medicine regularly.'
options: The doctor ordered the patient to take medicine regularly.
The doctor advised the patient to take medicine regularly.
The doctor advised the patient that take medicine regularly.
The doctor requested the patient taking medicine regularly.
exp: Imperative sentences giving medical advice use 'advised + object + to + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said to me, 'Please lend me your book.'
options: He ordered me to lend him my book.
He requested me to lend him my book.
He requested me that lend him my book.
He asked me please lend him my book.
exp: 'Please' changes the reporting verb to 'requested' and connects with 'to + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: Father said to his son, 'Do not waste your time.'
options: Father advised his son not to waste his time.
Father advised his son to not waste your time.
Father forbade his son not to waste his time.
Father told his son do not waste his time.
exp: Negative imperatives use 'advised/ordered + object + not to + V1' (or 'forbade + object + to + V1' without 'not').

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said, 'Alas! I am ruined.'
options: She exclaimed with joy that she was ruined.
She exclaimed with sorrow that she was ruined.
She said with sorrow that I am ruined.
She cried that she is ruined.
exp: Exclamatory word 'Alas!' expresses grief, changing to 'exclaimed with sorrow that...'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: The captain said, 'Hurrah! We have won the match.'
options: The captain exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
The captain said with joy that we have won the match.
The captain exclaimed with sorrow that they had won the match.
The captain shouted that they won the match.
exp: 'Hurrah!' indicates joy ('exclaimed with joy'), and 'have won' shifts to 'had won'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said, 'What a beautiful flower it is!'
options: He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful flower.
He asked what a beautiful flower it was.
He said that what a beautiful flower it is.
He exclaimed that it is a very beautiful flower.
exp: Exclamations beginning with 'What' or 'How' change into assertive statements using 'very' or 'great'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: My mother said to me, 'May God bless you!'
options: My mother prayed that God might bless me.
My mother said that God may bless you.
My mother wished me to God bless.
My mother prayed if God might bless me.
exp: Optative sentences expressing prayer use 'prayed that + subject + might + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He says, 'I am a student.'
options: He says that he was a student.
He says that he is a student.
He told that he is a student.
He says that I am a student.
exp: When the reporting verb is in the Present Tense ('says'), the tense of the reported speech does not change.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said to me, 'I have been waiting for you since morning.'
options: She told me that she has been waiting for me since morning.
She told me that she had been waiting for me since morning.
She asked me that she had been waiting for me since morning.
She told me that I had been waiting for her since morning.
exp: Present Perfect Continuous ('have been waiting') changes to Past Perfect Continuous ('had been waiting').

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: The master said to the servant, 'Bring a glass of water.'
options: The master requested the servant to bring a glass of water.
The master ordered the servant to bring a glass of water.
The master advised the servant bringing a glass of water.
The master told the servant that bring a glass of water.
exp: A command from a master to a servant uses 'ordered + object + to + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said to me, 'Can you solve this sum?'
options: He asked me if I could solve that sum.
He asked me if I can solve this sum.
He asked me that could I solve that sum.
He told me whether I could solve this sum.
exp: 'Can' changes to 'could', 'this' changes to 'that', and 'if' introduces the yes/no question.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: Mohan said, 'Let us go for a walk.'
options: Mohan proposed that they should go for a walk.
Mohan ordered that we go for a walk.
Mohan requested to go for a walk.
Mohan said that let us go for a walk.
exp: Suggestions starting with 'Let us' change to 'proposed/suggested that + they/we + should + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said, 'I must go now.'
options: She said that she must go now.
She said that she had to go then.
She said that she will go then.
She told that she must went then.
exp: 'Must' denoting present obligation changes to 'had to' in past indirect speech, and 'now' becomes 'then'.

q: Choose the correct direct narration: He asked me what my name was.
options: He said to me, 'What is your name?'
He said to me, 'What was your name?'
He said to me, 'What is my name?'
He told me, 'What your name is?'
exp: Indirect 'what my name was' reverses back to direct question 'What is your name?'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: The teacher said to the boys, 'Honesty is the best policy.'
options: The teacher told the boys that honesty was the best policy.
The teacher told the boys that honesty is the best policy.
The teacher asked the boys that honesty is the best policy.
The teacher said the boys honesty is the best policy.
exp: Proverbs retain their Simple Present Tense ('is') even when the reporting verb is past.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said to her, 'Why are you weeping?'
options: He asked her why was she weeping.
He asked her why she was weeping.
He asked her that why she was weeping.
He told her why she is weeping.
exp: Present Continuous ('are weeping') shifts to Past Continuous ('was weeping') in assertive order.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: Ravi said, 'I was reading a novel.'
options: Ravi said that he was reading a novel.
Ravi said that he had been reading a novel.
Ravi said that he is reading a novel.
Ravi told that he had read a novel.
exp: Past Continuous ('was reading') changes to Past Perfect Continuous ('had been reading').

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said to me, 'Have you finished your work?'
options: She asked me if I have finished my work.
She asked me if I had finished my work.
She asked me had I finished my work.
She told me whether I had finished your work.
exp: Present Perfect ('Have... finished') shifts to Past Perfect ('had finished').

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said, 'Good morning, my friend!'
options: He wished his friend good morning.
He said good morning to my friend.
He asked his friend good morning.
He told good morning to his friend.
exp: Greetings like 'Good morning' or 'Happy Birthday' use 'wished' as the reporting verb.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: The beggar said to me, 'Please give me something to eat.'
options: The beggar ordered me to give him something to eat.
The beggar requested me to give him something to eat.
The beggar prayed me to give him something to eat.
The beggar said me to give him something to eat.
exp: Polite pleas take 'requested + object + to + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said, 'I saw him two days ago.'
options: She said that she saw him two days ago.
She said that she had seen him two days before.
She said that she has seen him two days before.
She told that she had seen him two days ago.
exp: 'Saw' (V2) shifts to 'had seen' (had + V3), and 'ago' changes to 'before'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: They said, 'We love our country.'
options: They said that they loved their country.
They said that we loved our country.
They told that they love their country.
They said that they had loved their country.
exp: 'We' changes to 'they', 'love' to 'loved', and 'our' to 'their'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said to me, 'Did you attend the class yesterday?'
options: He asked me if I attended the class the previous day.
He asked me if I had attended the class the previous day.
He asked me did I attend the class yesterday.
He told me whether I had attended the class yesterday.
exp: Simple Past interrogative ('Did you attend') shifts to Past Perfect ('I had attended').

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: The old woman said, 'May you live long!'
options: The old woman blessed me that I might live long.
The old woman said that I may live long.
The old woman asked that I might live long.
The old woman ordered me to live long.
exp: Blessings use 'blessed/wished that + subject + might + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He will say, 'I am tired.'
options: He will say that he was tired.
He will say that he is tired.
He would say that he is tired.
He will tell that he is tired.
exp: When the reporting verb is in the Future Tense ('will say'), the tense inside quotation marks remains unchanged.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: Sita said to Ram, 'Let me go home.'
options: Sita requested Ram to let her go home.
Sita ordered Ram to let her go home.
Sita said Ram let her go home.
Sita proposed Ram that she should go home.
exp: 'Let me' expressing a request changes to 'requested + object + to let + pronoun + V1'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said, 'Two and two make four.'
options: He said that two and two made four.
He said that two and two make four.
He told that two and two makes four.
He said that two and two had made four.
exp: Mathematical truths do not change their tense in indirect narration.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: She said to me, 'Don't touch the wire.'
options: She warned me not to touch the wire.
She warned me to not touch the wire.
She forbade me not to touch the wire.
She said me don't touch the wire.
exp: Warnings in negative imperative take 'warned + object + not to + V1'.

q: In indirect speech, the word 'here' usually changes into:
exp: Words expressing nearness change into words expressing distance: 'here' becomes 'there', 'this' becomes 'that'.

q: In indirect speech, 'tonight' changes into:
exp: 'Today' changes to 'that day' and 'tonight' changes to 'that night'.

q: Choose the correct direct narration: She told me that she was happy.
options: She said to me, 'I am happy.'
She said to me, 'She was happy.'
She said to me, 'You are happy.'
exp: 'Told me' reverts to 'said to me' and 'she was' reverts to 'I am'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: He said, 'Bravo! You have done well.'
options: He applauded him saying that he had done well.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he had done well.
He shouted that you have done well.
He told him bravo you did well.
exp: 'Bravo!' expresses praise and changes to 'applauded... saying that...'.

q: Choose the correct indirect narration: My teacher said, 'Work hard if you want to pass.'
options: My teacher advised me to work hard if I wanted to pass.
My teacher ordered me work hard if you want to pass.
My teacher advised me to work hard if I want to pass.
My teacher told me that work hard if I wanted to pass.
exp: 'Work hard' becomes 'to work hard' and 'want' shifts to past tense 'wanted'.

q: We ______ obey the laws of our country.
exp: 'Must' expresses strong moral or legal obligation and duty.

q: ______ I come in, Sir?
exp: 'May' is the standard formal modal used to ask for permission politely.

q: He ______ swim across the river when he was young.
exp: 'Could' expresses past physical ability or capacity.

q: Work hard lest you ______ fail.
exp: The conjunction 'lest' is always followed by the modal auxiliary 'should'.

q: It is cloudy today; it ______ rain.
exp: 'May' indicates factual possibility based on present evidence (cloudy sky).

q: We ______ respect our parents and teachers.
exp: 'Ought to' (or 'should') expresses moral duty and social obligation.

q: ______ God bless you with success!
exp: 'May' is used at the beginning of optative sentences to express wishes, blessings, or prayers.

q: She ______ speak five languages fluently.
exp: 'Can' denotes present ability, skill, or capacity.

q: You ______ not enter my room without permission.
exp: 'Must not' expresses strict prohibition.

q: My grandfather ______ walk five miles every morning before his illness.
exp: 'Used to' expresses a discontinued past habit.

q: ______ you please lend me your pen for a minute?
exp: 'Could' (or 'Would') is used for making very polite requests.

q: You look very tired; you ______ take some rest.
exp: 'Should' is used to give friendly advice or suggestions.

q: How ______ you insult me in front of everyone?
exp: 'Dare' as a semi-modal means 'to have the courage/audacity to' in questions and negatives.

q: You ______ not worry; everything will be fine.
exp: 'Need not' expresses absence of necessity.

q: If I were a bird, I ______ fly in the sky.
exp: In imaginary Type-2 conditionals ('If I were...'), 'would' is used in the main clause.

q: The lights are on; someone ______ be inside the house.
exp: 'Must' expresses strong logical deduction or certainty based on evidence.

q: He ran fast so that he ______ catch the train.
exp: When the main clause is in the past tense ('ran'), 'so that' takes 'might' to show purpose.

q: We eat so that we ______ live.
exp: When the main clause is in the present tense ('eat'), 'so that' takes 'may'.

q: ______ you like a cup of hot tea?
exp: 'Would you like...' is the polite idiomatic form for offering something.

q: Candidates ______ bring their admit cards to the examination hall.
exp: Official rules and mandatory instructions use 'must'.

q: She ______ rather die than beg.
exp: 'Would rather... than' expresses strong personal preference.

q: I ______ help you if you tell me the truth.
exp: 'Will' with first person ('I/We') expresses promise, willingness, or determination.

q: You ______ have told me earlier; now it is too late.
exp: 'Should have + V3' expresses unfulfilled duty or regret about a past action.

q: He ______ not go there alone at night; it is dangerous.
exp: 'Dare not' (without 'to') indicates lack of courage.

q: ______ we go for a picnic this Sunday?
exp: 'Shall we...?' is used to make a suggestion or proposal involving the speaker and listener.

q: There ______ be a huge banyan tree here ten years ago.
exp: 'Used to' describes a past state or existence that is no longer true.

q: Nobody ______ challenge the laws of nature.
exp: 'Can' denotes universal capability or impossibility in negative statements.

q: Passengers ______ not smoke inside the train.
exp: Public safety prohibitions use 'must not'.

q: She said that she ______ come the next day.
exp: In indirect speech after a past reporting verb ('said'), 'will' shifts to 'would'.

q: Even a child ______ solve this simple riddle.
exp: 'Can' expresses theoretical possibility or ease of doing something.

q: He ______ be at home now, though I am not completely sure.
exp: 'Might' expresses weak or remote possibility.

q: We ______ love our neighbours.
exp: 'Ought to' takes 'to + V1' to express ethical duty.

q: How many primary auxiliary verbs are there in English grammar?
exp: The three primary auxiliaries are 'Be' (is, am, are, was, were), 'Do' (do, does, did), and 'Have' (has, have, had).

q: Which of the following is a semi-modal (marginal modal) verb?
exp: 'Dare', 'Need', and 'Used to' behave both as main verbs and modal auxiliaries, hence called semi-modals.

q: Do modal auxiliaries change their form according to the number or person of the subject?
options: No, they remain invariant (e.g., He can, They can)
exp: Modal verbs never take '-s', '-es', '-ing', or '-ed' endings.

q: Which form of the main verb immediately follows a pure modal auxiliary (like can, must, should)?
exp: Pure modals are always followed directly by the base form (V1) of the verb without 'to'.

q: She ______ to finish this assignment before 5 PM.
exp: Because 'to' is present before 'finish', 'has' ('has to') is grammatically required.

q: If you heat ice, it ______ melt.
exp: Predictable scientific consequences use 'will'.

q: I am sure he ______ pass with flying colours.
exp: 'Will' expresses strong confidence or prediction about the future.

q: ______ you mind closing the window?
exp: 'Would you mind + V-ing...?' is a standard polite request formula.

q: The cat jumped ______ the table.
exp: 'Upon' (or 'onto') indicates upward movement onto a surface.

q: He died ______ cholera last night.
exp: When a person dies directly from a disease, the fixed preposition 'of' ('died of cholera/cancer') is used.

q: She is fond ______ classical music.
exp: The adjective 'fond' always takes the fixed preposition 'of'.

q: The frog jumped ______ the well.
exp: 'Into' denotes motion from outside to inside an enclosed space.

q: He is senior ______ me by two years.
exp: Latin comparatives ending in '-ior' (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior) always take 'to' instead of 'than'.

q: Distribute these sweets ______ the two brothers.
exp: 'Between' is used for two persons or things, whereas 'among' is used for more than two.

q: Distribute the mangoes ______ all the students of the class.
exp: 'Among' is used when referring to more than two individuals or a group.

q: I prefer tea ______ coffee.
exp: The verb 'prefer' takes the fixed preposition 'to' when comparing two nouns.

q: He has been living in Delhi ______ 2015.
exp: 'Since' is used before a specific point of time (e.g., 2015, Monday, morning).

q: She has been waiting here ______ three hours.
exp: 'For' is used before a period or duration of time (e.g., three hours, ten days).

q: The lion was killed ______ the hunter ______ a gun.
exp: 'By' denotes the doer/agent ('the hunter') and 'with' denotes the instrument used ('a gun').

q: Beware ______ pickpockets in crowded buses.
exp: 'Beware' is always followed by the fixed preposition 'of'.

q: He is good ______ mathematics.
exp: To show skill or proficiency in a subject or activity, 'good at' is the standard fixed usage.

q: She is afraid ______ dogs.
exp: 'Afraid' always takes the fixed preposition 'of'.

q: The train arrived ______ the station on time.
exp: 'At' is used for specific points and smaller places like a railway station or bus stop.

q: We should abstain ______ bad habits.
exp: The verb 'abstain' is always followed by the preposition 'from'.

q: He is proud ______ his achievements.
exp: 'Proud' takes 'of' ('pride' as a noun takes 'in').

q: The book is lying ______ the table.
exp: 'On' indicates rest in contact with a surface.

q: Look ______ the blackboard carefully.
exp: 'Look at' means to direct one's gaze towards something.

q: She is suffering ______ high fever.
exp: 'Suffer' always takes the preposition 'from'.

q: Do not laugh ______ the poor.
exp: 'Laugh at' means to mock or ridicule someone.

q: He congratulated me ______ my grand success.
exp: The verb 'congratulate' always takes the fixed preposition 'on'.

q: The bridge was built ______ the Ganga river.
exp: 'Over' indicates something spanning directly above from one side to the other.

q: He agrees ______ my proposal.
exp: 'Agree with' is used for a person, whereas 'agree to' is used for a proposal, plan, or suggestion.

q: I agree ______ you on this matter.
exp: 'Agree with' is always used when referring to a person.

q: She was born ______ 15th August.
exp: 'On' is used before specific dates and days of the week.

q: Gandhiji was born ______ 1869.
exp: 'In' is used before months, years, seasons, and centuries.

q: He is blind ______ one eye.
exp: 'Blind in one eye' is used for physical blindness, whereas 'blind to' means ignoring faults.

q: A mother is often blind ______ her son's faults.
exp: 'Blind to' means unwilling or unable to notice flaws.

q: Listen ______ what your teacher says.
exp: The verb 'listen' is always followed by the preposition 'to'.

q: He dealt ______ his customers politely.
exp: 'Deal with' means to behave towards or handle people/problems, while 'deal in' means to trade in goods.

q: My uncle deals ______ rice and wheat.
exp: 'Deal in' refers to trading or doing business in a commodity.

q: The aeroplane flew ______ the clouds.
exp: 'Above' indicates a higher position without direct physical contact.

q: He is knocking ______ the door.
exp: 'Knock at the door' is standard idiomatic British and Indian English usage.

q: Please pay attention ______ your studies.
exp: 'Pay attention to' is a fixed prepositional collocation.

q: She is married ______ a doctor.
exp: In passive/adjectival constructions, 'married' always takes 'to' (never 'with').

q: He accused his neighbour ______ theft.
exp: The verb 'accuse' takes the fixed preposition 'of'.

q: We rely ______ our parents for guidance.
exp: 'Rely' (like 'depend') is always followed by 'on' or 'upon'.

q: The dog ran ______ the road.
exp: 'Across' indicates movement from one side of a road or river to the opposite side.

q: He is eligible ______ this government post.
exp: 'Eligible' is always followed by the preposition 'for'.

q: He is ______ honest man.
exp: 'Honest' begins with a silent 'h' and produces a vowel sound ('o'), so 'an' is used.

q: My elder brother is ______ M.A. in English.
exp: The abbreviation 'M.A.' starts with a vowel sound ('em'), so 'an' is used before it.

q: She wants to become ______ engineer.
exp: 'Engineer' begins with a vowel sound ('e'), so the indefinite article 'an' is correct.

q: ______ Ganga is a sacred river of India.
exp: The definite article 'The' is always used before the names of famous rivers like the Ganga.

q: He is ______ university professor.
exp: 'University' begins with a consonant sound ('yu'), therefore 'a' is used instead of 'an'.

q: I saw ______ one-eyed man on the road yesterday.
exp: 'One' begins with the consonant sound 'wa', so 'a' is used before 'one-eyed man'.

q: ______ sun rises in the east.
exp: Unique heavenly bodies like the sun, the moon, and the earth take the definite article 'The'.

q: Kalidas is known as ______ Shakespeare of India.
exp: When a proper noun is used as a common noun for comparison, 'the' is placed before it.

q: Gold is ______ precious metal.
exp: 'Precious metal' is a singular countable noun phrase starting with a consonant sound, taking 'a'.

q: ______ Ramayana is a great religious epic.
exp: 'The' is always used before the names of sacred scriptures and epics like the Ramayana and the Gita.

q: Can you play ______ harmonium well?
exp: The definite article 'the' is used before the names of musical instruments when referring to playing them.

q: He arrived ______ hour late for the meeting.
exp: 'Hour' has a silent 'h' and starts with a vowel sound ('our'), requiring 'an'.

q: Mount Everest is ______ highest peak in the world.
exp: Superlative degree adjectives like 'highest' always take 'the' before them.

q: ______ honesty is the best policy.
exp: Abstract nouns used in a general sense do not take any article before them.

q: She gave me ______ useful piece of advice.
exp: 'Useful' begins with a consonant sound ('yu'), so 'a' is used.

q: ______ rich should help the poor.
exp: When an adjective represents a whole class of people (the rich, the poor), 'The' is used before it.

q: Copper is ______ useful metal.
exp: Because 'useful' starts with the 'yu' sound, 'a' is the right article.

q: He met with ______ accident near the station.
exp: 'Accident' starts with a vowel sound ('a'), so 'an' is used.

q: ______ Himalayas lie to the north of India.
exp: 'The' is used before the names of mountain ranges like the Himalayas and the Alps.

q: Please give me ______ glass of cold water.
exp: 'Glass' is a singular countable noun starting with a consonant sound, so 'a' is used.

q: I have ______ headache today.
exp: Fixed expressions like 'a headache', 'a cold', and 'a fever' take the indefinite article 'a'.

q: ______ more you read, the more you learn.
exp: In parallel comparative constructions ('The more... the more'), 'The' is used before both comparatives.

q: He is ______ European citizen.
exp: 'European' begins with the consonant sound 'yu', so 'a' is used.

q: Do not make ______ noise in the class.
exp: 'Make a noise' is a standard idiomatic phrase requiring 'a'.

q: ______ Taj Mahal is one of the wonders of the world.
exp: Famous historical monuments and buildings take 'The' before their names.

q: He reads ______ Times of India every morning.
exp: 'The' is placed before the names of newspapers and magazines.

q: Iron is ______ heavy metal.
exp: 'Heavy' begins with a consonant 'h' sound, so 'a' is used.

q: She is ______ heir to a vast property.
exp: 'Heir' is pronounced like 'air' (silent 'h'), so it takes 'an'.

q: ______ water in this well is very sweet.
exp: Although 'water' is uncountable, here it refers to specific water in a particular well, requiring 'The'.

q: He goes to school on ______ foot.
exp: No article is used in the prepositional phrase 'on foot'.

q: Sri Lanka is ______ island in the Indian Ocean.
exp: 'Island' begins with a vowel sound ('ai'), so 'an' is used.

q: My father is ______ S.D.O. in this district.
exp: 'S.D.O.' starts with a vowel sound ('es'), therefore 'an' is correct.

q: ______ gold of South Africa is famous worldwide.
exp: When a material noun is particularized ('gold of South Africa'), 'The' is used.

q: We drink ______ milk every day.
exp: Material nouns used in a general sense do not take any article.

q: ______ man is mortal.
exp: When 'man' or 'woman' is used in the broadest sense to represent all humanity, no article is used.

q: This is ______ best book on English grammar.
exp: Superlative adjective 'best' requires 'the' before it.

q: What ______ beautiful painting it is!
exp: In exclamatory sentences starting with 'What' followed by a singular countable noun, 'a' or 'an' is used.

q: He has been suffering from fever since ______ Monday.
exp: Names of days and months do not take any article before them.

q: ______ Andamans are a group of islands in the Bay of Bengal.
exp: 'The' is used before the names of groups of islands like the Andamans and the West Indies.

q: Never tell ______ lie.
exp: 'Tell a lie' is a fixed English idiom requiring the indefinite article 'a'.

q: Bread and butter ______ my favourite breakfast.
exp: When two nouns joined by 'and' express a single unit or food item ('bread and butter'), a singular verb ('is') is used.

q: Slow and steady ______ the race.
exp: Proverbial phrases expressing a single unified idea take a singular verb ('wins').

q: Each of the boys ______ given a prize.
exp: 'Each of', 'Either of', and 'Neither of' are followed by a plural noun/pronoun, but always take a singular verb ('was').

q: Neither Ram nor his friends ______ present today.
exp: With 'Neither... nor' and 'Either... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject ('his friends' - plural), taking 'are'.

q: The poet and philosopher ______ dead.
exp: When 'the' is used only once before two nouns joined by 'and', both refer to the same person, requiring a singular verb ('is').

q: The poet and the philosopher ______ arrived.
exp: When 'the' is repeated before both nouns, they refer to two different individuals, taking a plural verb ('have').

q: A number of students ______ absent yesterday.
exp: 'A number of + plural noun' takes a plural verb ('were'), whereas 'The number of' takes a singular verb.

q: The number of students in this class ______ fifty.
exp: 'The number of' refers to a specific singular figure, so it always takes a singular verb ('is').

q: Many a man ______ ruined by gambling.
exp: 'Many a/an' is followed by a singular countable noun and always takes a singular verb ('is').

q: Ram, as well as his parents, ______ coming.
exp: When two subjects are joined by 'as well as', 'with', or 'along with', the verb agrees with the first subject ('Ram' - singular).

q: Mathematics ______ a very interesting subject.
exp: Names of subjects ending in '-ics' (Mathematics, Physics, Economics) are singular in meaning and take a singular verb ('is').

q: Fifty miles ______ a long distance to walk.
exp: A specific distance, weight, or sum of money considered as a whole unit takes a singular verb ('is').

q: The jury ______ divided in their opinions.
exp: When a collective noun ('jury') acts as divided individuals ('their opinions'), a plural verb ('were') is used.

q: The jury ______ unanimous in its decision.
exp: When a collective noun acts as a single unified body ('its decision'), it takes a singular verb ('was').

q: One of my friends ______ in London.
exp: 'One of + plural noun' always takes a singular verb ('lives').

q: Cattle ______ grazing in the green field.
exp: 'Cattle', 'police', 'people', and 'peasantry' look singular but are always plural in usage, taking 'are'.

q: The news ______ too good to be true.
exp: 'News' looks plural because of '-s', but it is an uncountable singular noun taking 'is'.

q: Either you or I ______ to blame.
exp: With 'Either... or', the verb agrees with the nearest subject ('I'), taking 'am'.

q: Time and tide ______ for none.
exp: 'Time and tide' represent two distinct forces, taking the plural verb 'wait'.

q: Everyone in the hall ______ silent.
exp: Indefinite pronouns like 'everyone', 'someone', 'nobody', and 'each' always take a singular verb ('was').

q: The Arabian Nights ______ a famous book of stories.
exp: Titles of books, even if plural in form, always take a singular verb ('is').

q: The quality of these mangoes ______ not good.
exp: The actual subject is 'The quality' (singular), not 'mangoes', so 'is' is correct.

q: My spectacles ______ broken.
exp: Nouns consisting of two inseparable parts (spectacles, scissors, trousers) take a plural verb ('are').

q: A pair of shoes ______ lying under the bed.
exp: When preceded by 'A pair of', the subject becomes singular ('pair'), taking 'is'.

q: If I ______ rich, I would help the needy.
exp: Hypothetical 'if' clauses always use 'were' for all subjects.

q: Gold and silver ______ precious metals.
exp: Two distinct material nouns joined by 'and' take a plural verb ('are').

q: None of the boys ______ completed the task.
exp: In modern usage with plural countable nouns ('boys'), 'None of' commonly takes a plural verb ('have').

q: More than one boy ______ punished.
exp: 'More than one' is followed by a singular noun and takes a singular verb ('was').

q: The captain with all his sailors ______ drowned.
exp: Phrases introduced by 'with' do not affect the number of the main subject ('The captain' - singular).

q: Rice and curry ______ his usual lunch.
exp: 'Rice and curry' forms a single dish, requiring a singular verb ('is').

q: The rich ______ not always happy.
exp: 'The + adjective' ('The rich') denotes a plural class of people, taking 'are'.

q: Nothing but trees ______ seen in the forest.
exp: 'Nothing but' is always followed by a singular verb ('was') regardless of the noun after 'but'.

q: Every boy and every girl ______ given a certificate.
exp: When two singular nouns joined by 'and' are preceded by 'each' or 'every', the verb is singular ('was').

q: Five thousand rupees ______ a big amount for a poor man.
exp: A lump sum of money takes a singular verb ('is').

q: There ______ many books in our school library.
exp: With introductory 'There', the verb agrees with the real subject following it ('many books' - plural).

q: Gulliver's Travels ______ written by Jonathan Swift.
exp: The title of a novel is singular, so 'was' is used.

q: Neither of the two roads ______ safe at night.
exp: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb ('is').

q: He is one of those writers who ______ won worldwide fame.
exp: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to its plural antecedent 'writers', so 'have' is correct.

q: The furniture in this room ______ very old.
exp: 'Furniture', 'scenery', 'luggage', and 'information' are uncountable singular nouns taking 'is'.

q: Either Sita or Gita ______ stolen my pen.
exp: Two singular subjects joined by 'Either... or' take a singular verb ('has').

q: Choose the correct combination: 'He is very weak. He cannot walk.'
options: He is so weak to walk.
He is too weak to walk.
He is very weak for walking.
He is too weak that he cannot walk.
exp: Combining two sentences using 'too... to' yields 'He is too weak to walk'.

q: Remove 'too' from the sentence: 'She is too proud to beg.'
options: She is so proud that she will not beg.
She is so proud that she cannot beg.
She is very proud to beg.
She is proud so she begs.
exp: 'Too + adjective + to + V1' transforms into 'so + adjective + that + subject + cannot/could not + V1'.

q: Choose the correct negative sentence without changing meaning: 'Man is mortal.'
exp: Affirmative to negative transformation uses 'not' + antonym ('mortal' -> 'immortal').

q: Choose the correct negative sentence: 'Only a fool would say so.'
options: None but a fool would say so.
Only not a fool would say so.
Nobody is a fool to say so.
exp: 'Only' or 'Alone' at the start of an affirmative sentence changes into 'None but' in negative transformation.

q: Choose the correct negative sentence: 'As soon as the thief saw the police, he ran away.'
options: No sooner did the thief see the police than he ran away.
No sooner had the thief saw the police than he ran away.
No sooner did the thief saw the police when he ran away.
Hardly the thief saw the police than he ran away.
exp: 'As soon as' transforms into 'No sooner did + subject + V1 + than...'.

q: Choose the correct assertive sentence: 'Who can touch pitch without being defiled?'
options: Nobody can touch pitch without being defiled.
exp: A rhetorical affirmative question starting with 'Who' converts into an assertive statement starting with 'Nobody/No one'.

q: Choose the correct exclamatory sentence: 'It is a very beautiful night.'
options: What a beautiful night it is!
exp: When 'a/an + adjective + singular noun' is present, the exclamation begins with 'What a/an...'.

q: Choose the correct assertive sentence: 'How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank!'
options: The moonlight sleeps very sweetly upon this bank.
exp: Exclamatory 'How + adverb/adjective' transforms into 'very + adverb/adjective' in assertive form.

q: Choose the correct combination: 'He worked hard. He failed.'
options: Though he worked hard, he failed.
He worked hard because he failed.
He worked hard so he failed.
exp: Contrasting ideas are combined using 'Though/Although' or 'but' ('Though he worked hard, he failed').

q: Choose the correct combination: 'The sun rose. The fog dispersed.'
options: The sun having risen, the fog dispersed.
The sun rising, fog had dispersed.
exp: Using a nominative absolute participle ('The sun having risen') cleanly combines two sequential events.

q: Choose the correct comparative degree: 'Ram is as strong as Shyam.'
options: Shyam is not stronger than Ram.
Shyam is less strong than Ram.
exp: Positive 'as... as' transforms into negative comparative 'not + comparative + than' without changing meaning.

q: Choose the correct positive degree: 'Gold is more precious than silver.'
options: Silver is as precious as gold.
Silver is not so precious as gold.
Gold is not so precious as silver.
Silver is more precious than gold.
exp: Affirmative comparative ('X is more... than Y') changes to negative positive ('Y is not so... as X').

q: Choose the correct superlative degree: 'No other metal is so useful as iron.'
options: Iron is the most useful of all metals.
Iron is more useful than any metal.
Iron is one of the most useful metals.
exp: 'No other... so + positive + as' converts into 'the + superlative' ('the most useful').

q: Choose the correct combination: 'This is the boy. He won the first prize.'
options: This is the boy which won the first prize.
This is the boy who won the first prize.
This is the boy whom won the first prize.
This is the boy whose won the first prize.
exp: Relative pronoun 'who' combines two clauses referring to a person as the subject.

q: Choose the correct combination: 'He is poor. He is honest.'
options: He is poor, yet he is honest.
He is poor because he is honest.
He is poor so he is honest.
exp: 'Yet' (or 'but') combines two contrasting qualities into a compound sentence.

q: Choose the correct complex sentence: 'Tell me the truth.'
options: Tell me what the truth is.
exp: Expanding the noun phrase 'the truth' into a noun clause ('what the truth is') forms a complex sentence.

q: Choose the correct simple sentence: 'He finished his work and went home.'
options: Having finished his work, he went home.
When he finished his work, he went home.
He finished his work so he went home.
After he finished work, he went home.
exp: Using a perfect participle ('Having finished') converts a compound sentence into a single-clause simple sentence.

q: Choose the correct combination: 'I saw a man. He was blind.'
options: I saw a man and blind.
I saw a man which was blind.
exp: Using the adjective 'blind' directly before 'man' combines the two simple sentences concisely.

q: Choose the correct transformation into interrogative: 'Everybody loves his motherland.'
options: Who does not love his motherland?
exp: Affirmative 'Everybody' transforms into a rhetorical negative question 'Who does not...?'.

q: Choose the correct combination: 'Walk carefully. You will fall down.'
options: Walk carefully lest you should fall down.
Walk carefully because you will fall down.
Walk carefully so you fall down.
exp: 'Lest... should' combines an instruction with a warning against an undesirable consequence.

q: Choose the correct negative sentence: 'I always remember you.'
exp: 'Always' changes to 'never' and 'remember' changes to its antonym 'forget'.

q: Choose the correct combination: 'He had no money. He could not buy food.'
options: Having no money, he could not buy food.
He had no money yet bought food.
He could buy food without money.
No money had he to buy food.
exp: Participle phrase 'Having no money' expresses cause smoothly.

q: Choose the correct combination: 'She is too tired. She cannot run.'
options: She is too tired to run.
She is very tired to run.
She is so tired to run.
She is tired enough to run.
exp: 'Too + adjective + to + V1' combines the cause and negative result.

q: Choose the correct compound sentence: 'In spite of being rich, he is unhappy.'
options: He is rich, still he is unhappy.
Because he is rich, he is unhappy.
Though he is rich, he is unhappy.
exp: Coordinating conjunction 'still' or 'but' creates a compound sentence (whereas 'Though' creates a complex sentence).

q: Choose the correct combination: 'This is the place. Gandhiji was born here.'
options: This is the place which Gandhiji was born.
This is the place where Gandhiji was born.
This is the place when Gandhiji was born.
This is the place who Gandhiji was born.
exp: Relative adverb 'where' connects a clause referring to a place.

q: Choose the correct negative sentence: 'Every rose has a thorn.'
options: There is no rose without a thorn.
exp: 'Every X has Y' transforms into 'There is no X without Y'.

q: Choose the correct combination: 'He will pass. It is certain.'
options: It is certain that he will pass.
He will pass because it is certain.
exp: A noun clause introduced by 'that' combines both statements smoothly.

q: Choose the correct transformation: 'He is too honest to accept a bribe.'
options: He is so honest that he cannot accept a bribe.
He is so honest that he will accept a bribe.
He is very honest for accepting a bribe.
He is honest enough to accept a bribe.

q: Which period is known as the 'Old English' (Anglo-Saxon) period in the history of English literature?
exp: The Old English period stretches from the Anglo-Saxon invasion in AD 449 to the Norman Conquest in AD 1066.

q: Which three Germanic tribes invaded Britain in the 5th century AD and laid the foundation of the English language?
exp: The Angles, Saxons, and Jutes came from northern Germany and Denmark; 'England' derives from 'Angle-land'.

q: What is the oldest surviving epic poem in Old English literature?
exp: 'Beowulf' is the greatest surviving heroic epic of the Old English period.

q: Which historic event in AD 1066 marked the end of the Old English period and introduced massive French vocabulary into English?
exp: William the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold in 1066, bringing Norman-French rule to England.

q: Which period is recognized as the 'Middle English' period?
exp: Middle English spans roughly from AD 1150 to AD 1500, bridging Old English and Modern English.

q: Who is hailed as the 'Father of English Poetry' and the greatest writer of the Middle English period?
exp: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400), author of 'The Canterbury Tales', established the East Midland dialect as standard English.

q: Which dialect of Middle English eventually evolved into Standard Modern English?
exp: Spoken in London, Oxford, and Cambridge, and used by Chaucer and Caxton, the East Midland dialect became Standard English.

q: Who set up the first printing press in England at Westminster in AD 1476?
exp: William Caxton introduced the printing press to England in 1476, helping standardize English spelling and grammar.

q: Which major phonetic change occurred between Middle English and Modern English, altering the pronunciation of long vowels?
exp: The Great Vowel Shift (15th–17th centuries) transformed English vowel pronunciation and explains why English spelling differs from pronunciation.

q: From which year does the 'Modern English' period begin?
exp: Modern English begins around AD 1500 with the Renaissance, printing press, and overseas expansion.

q: Which two major historical movements enriched Modern English with thousands of Latin and Greek words?
options: The Stone Age and Bronze Age
exp: The revival of classical learning during the Renaissance brought vast Latin and Greek vocabulary into English.

q: Who is universally regarded as the greatest dramatist and poet of the Early Modern English (Elizabethan) period?
exp: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) coined hundreds of words and idioms that remain central to English today.

q: Which landmark English translation of the Bible published in 1611 deeply influenced English prose style?
exp: The King James Version of 1611 became a cornerstone of Modern English prose and idioms.

q: Who compiled and published the first comprehensive 'Dictionary of the English Language' in 1755?
exp: Dr. Samuel Johnson published his monumental dictionary in 1755, fixing English spellings and definitions.

q: Who published 'An American Dictionary of the English Language' in 1828, standardizing American English spellings (like 'color' and 'center')?
exp: Noah Webster reformed American English spelling to distinguish it from British spelling.

q: To which major language family does English genetically belong?
exp: English belongs to the West Germanic branch of the Indo-European family of languages.

q: Which Anglo-Saxon king is called the 'Father of English Prose' for translating Latin works into Old English?
exp: King Alfred the Great promoted English learning and prose translations in the 9th century.

q: What script was used to write Old English before the adoption of the Roman alphabet?
exp: Early Anglo-Saxons carved inscriptions using the Germanic Runic alphabet before Christian missionaries introduced the Roman script.

q: Why was Old English grammar much more complex than Modern English grammar?
options: Because it was a highly inflected language with complex noun cases, grammatical genders, and verb endings
Because it was spoken only by kings
exp: Old English relied on word endings (inflections) rather than word order to show grammatical relationships.

q: Which three languages were simultaneously used in England during the Middle English period?
options: French (by the ruling court), Latin (by the Church), and English (by the common people)
exp: Trilingualism existed in medieval England until English re-emerged as the official national language in the 14th century.

q: Who wrote 'Piers Plowman', a famous allegorical poem of the Middle English period?
exp: William Langland wrote 'Piers Plowman', while John Gower wrote 'Confessio Amantis'.

q: Who wrote 'Paradise Lost', the greatest epic poem in Modern English?
exp: John Milton published 'Paradise Lost' in 1667 in majestic blank verse.

q: Which Indian English novelist wrote 'Untouchable' and 'Coolie'?
exp: Mulk Raj Anand, R. K. Narayan, and Raja Rao are the founding trio of Indian English fiction.

q: Who wrote the famous Indian English novel 'The Guide' and created the fictional town of Malgudi?
exp: R. K. Narayan won the Sahitya Akademi Award for 'The Guide' (1958).

q: Who is the author of 'Kanthapura' and 'The Serpent and the Rope'?
exp: Raja Rao's 'Kanthapura' (1938) brilliantly captures Gandhian nationalism in an Indian village.

q: Which Indian poet won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for the English translation of 'Gitanjali'?
exp: Rabindranath Tagore became the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature in 1913.

q: Who is famously known as the 'Nightingale of India' (Bharat Kokila) for her lyrical English poetry?
exp: Sarojini Naidu wrote acclaimed poetry collections like 'The Golden Threshold' and 'The Bird of Time'.

q: Who wrote the epic spiritual poem 'Savitri' in Indian English?
exp: Sri Aurobindo composed 'Savitri: A Legend and a Symbol' in blank verse.

q: Why is English called a 'Global Language' or 'World Language' today?
options: Because it is spoken only in England
Because it serves as the primary international medium for science, technology, diplomacy, aviation, trade, and the internet
Because it has the smallest vocabulary
exp: English is spoken across every continent as a first, second, or foreign language.

q: What is the main reason behind the global spread of English from the 17th to the 20th century?
options: The expansion of the British Empire followed by American economic and technological influence
exp: British colonialism spread English worldwide, while American scientific and digital dominance cemented its global role.

q: Which of the following is an English word borrowed from Hindi/Indian languages?

exp: English has freely absorbed words like jungle, bungalow, guru, veranda, and shampoo from Indian languages.

q: What is the key difference between British English and American English in the spelling of words like 'colour' and 'honour'?
exp: British '-our' corresponds to American '-or' (colour/color, labour/labor).

exp: British 'Autumn' corresponds to American 'Fall' (just as 'lift' corresponds to 'elevator').

q: Who wrote the famous morality play 'Everyman' during the Middle English period?
exp: 'Everyman' is the finest surviving medieval English morality play by an anonymous author.

q: Which four dialects existed during the Old English period?
options: Northumbrian, Mercian, West Saxon, and Kentish
exp: Old English had four main regional dialects: Northumbrian, Mercian, West Saxon, and Kentish.

q: In which dialect of Old English were most surviving manuscripts preserved due to King Alfred's patronage?
exp: West Saxon became the literary standard of Old English under King Alfred.

q: Who is known as the 'Father of Modern English Drama' (author of 'Pygmalion' and 'Arms and the Man')?
exp: G. B. Shaw revolutionized modern English theatre with his witty plays of ideas.

q: Which American poet wrote 'Leaves of Grass' and 'Song of Myself'?

options: It acts as a link language connecting diverse states and a window to global knowledge, science, and employment
It is spoken only in villages
It has replaced all regional languages
exp: English functions as an associate official language and a vital bridge for higher education and global communication in India.

q: What quality makes the English language uniquely adaptable and rich?
options: Its strict refusal to borrow words
Its openness to absorbing vocabulary from hundreds of languages around the world
exp: English's willingness to borrow and assimilate foreign words gives it one of the richest vocabularies in the world.
